item.title: How do you say levocetirizine (Xyzal)? (Pronunciation Series Episode 81)
item.description: We covered cetirizine in episode 304. Now, we're adding "levo," and talking about levocetirizine today. This is the 81st episode in my drug pronunciation series. We talk about pronunciations, not pharmacology. If you want to feel less frustrated learning drug names and sound more confident saying them, follow this series. Levocetirizine = LEE voe se TIR i zeen LEE, like Bruce Lee (the famous actor) voe, like vocation se, like citrus TIR, like Artificial Tears are over-the-counter lubricating eye drops. i (ih), which is a short "I" sound (schwa "I" sound). It's like the "I" in the word, "president." zeen, which rhymes with teen Emphasize LEE and TIR. TIR gets the most emphasis. Written pronunciation examples: USP Dictionary Online and MedlinePlus.gov Spoken pronunciation example: Tony PharmD's YouTube channel Xyzal = xy-ZAL xy, like xylophone ZAL, which rhymes with stall, like a horse stall. No literature says which syllable to emphasize. I tend to emphasize "zal." Written pronunciation source: I made this one up. Spoken pronunciation example: Xyzal YouTube channel. "Be wise all. Take Xyzal." https://links.thepharmacistsvoice.com/xzyalyoutubevideo Thank you for listening to episode 385 of The Pharmacist's Voice Podcast. item.title: How do you say ibuprofen? (Pronunciation Series Episode 80)
item.description: A small substitution can make a big difference to your ear. The official pronunciation for ibuprofen is EYE-bue-PROE-fen. Notice the second syllable, "bue." I have been saying "bee" instead of "bue" for decades. I first became aware of the official pronunciation in 2020, when I looked it up in the USP Dictionary Online. The way I say it is "in the ballpark." It's close enough, but it's not technically correct. As I recorded this episode, I felt uncomfortable admitting my decades-long mistake and owning the fact that I choose to say ibuprofen wrong even though I know better. I just feel more comfortable saying EYE-bee-PROE-fen. A lot of people say EYE-bee-PROE-fen instead of EYE-bue-PROE-fen. That doesn't make it right, but I'm happy to say that both variations sound about the same when said quickly. Pick your pronunciation, and own it when you say it! This is the 80th episode in my drug pronunciation series. We talk about pronunciations, not pharmacology. If you want to feel less frustrated learning drug names and sound more confident saying them, follow this series. Ibuprofen = EYE-bue-PROE-fen EYE, like eyeglasses bue, like butane (My variation is "bee," like a bumblebee.") PROE, like a the abbreviation for "professional." item.title: How do you say dextroamphetamine (Dexedrine)? (Pronunciation Series Episode 79)
item.description: This is the 79th episode in my drug pronunciation series. In this episode, I divide dextroamphetamine and Dexedrine into syllables, tell you which syllables to emphasize, and list my sources. We cover pronunciations, not pharmacology. If you want to feel less frustrated learning drug names and sound more confident saying them, follow this series. Dextroamphetamine = DEX-troe-am-FET-a-meen DEX, as in "dexter," the Latin word meaning "right." (Right as opposed to left.) Troe, like a Trojan Horse am, as in I am an Ohio-licensed pharmacist FET, like fetch (For example, "Jack and Jill went up the hill to fetch a pail of water.") A (uh), which is a short "A" sound, like the "A" in the word "adoption" (uh) meen, as in bullies are mean. Emphasize DEX and FET. FET gets the most emphasis. Written pronunciation source: USP Dictionary Online https://links.thepharmacistsvoice.com/uspdictionaryonline Spoken pronunciation example: Merriam Webster's Online Dictionary and Tony PharmD's YouTube Channel https://links.thepharmacistsvoice.com/tonypharmddextroamphetamine Dexedrine = dek-suh-drin dek, like a deck of cards suh, like supper drin, which rhymes with thin. In the literature, no emphasis is indicated on any syllable. I tend to emphasize "dek." item.title: How do you say abciximab? (Pronunciation Series Episode 74)
item.description: This is the 74th episode in my drug pronunciation series. In this episode, I divide abciximab into syllables, tell you which syllable to emphasize, and list my sources. ❌ We don't cover pharmacology in this series. Just pronunciations. How do you say abciximab? abciximab = ab-SIX-i-mab, ab, like abdomen SIX, like the number 6 i, which is a short "I" sound, like the "I" in the word, "president" (sounds like, "ih") mab, which is the stem for monoclonal antibodies Emphasize SIX Sources: USP Dictionary Online or drugs.com When I was a hospital pharmacy intern in the 90s, I didn't know how to say abciximab. It was a relatively new drug name at the time, and I kinda spelled it out instead of saying it. I just need to hear it once. Then, I knew how to say it forevermore. Why pick abciximab for the series? Even though my sources say that abciximab (ReoPro) has been discontinued in the US, it is still discussed among healthcare professionals and mentioned in printed resources. Therefore, the pronunciation is worth knowing. You may hear someone say it during your lifetime, and this podcast episode will help you connect the printed name with the spoken name. Plus, if you spell out drug names because you don't know how to say them, you might relate to this episode. I know what it's like to feel insecure saying something I have never heard before. item.title: 30 Episodes in 30 Days: My NaPodPoMo Challenge
item.description: November is National Podcast Post Month (NaPodPoMo), and I'm participating! NaPodPoMo is a challenge to publish 30 podcast episodes in 30 days. After six years of weekly episodes, The Pharmacist's Voice Podcast became a monthly show in January 2026. For November only, I'm picking up the pace: 30 episodes in 30 days! Thank you to Jennifer Navarrete for creating this fun challenge! Learn more at napodpomo.org. I successfully completed the challenge in November 2020. Can I do it again? Subscribe to/follow The Pharmacist's Voice Podcast on your favorite podcast app or on YouTube to find out! In today's episode, you'll hear why I'm taking on the challenge again, what I learned in 2020, and what's coming, including short drug pronunciation episodes, an interview about AI-driven drug naming, a tribute to Veteran pharmacists, and a milestone celebration. If all goes well, episode 400 comes out on November 25, 2026! Thank you for listening to episode 376 of The Pharmacist's Voice ® Podcast. If you know someone who would like this episode, please share it with them! Sign up for The Pharmacist's Voice ® monthly email newsletter! https://links.thepharmacistsvoice.com/newsletter Host Background: Kim Newlove has been an Ohio pharmacist since 2001 (BS Pharm, Chem Minor).
